summary: Specifies how defects are mapped and signaled between a pseudowire and the attachment circuits of the end-to-end service it emulates. It standardizes provider edge behavior for ATM, Frame Relay, TDM, and SONET/SDH services carried over MPLS and similar networks.

plainLanguage.summary: A pseudowire carries an older kind of connection, such as ATM or Frame Relay, across a modern packet network. If the customer line or the tunnel breaks, the routers at both ends have to find out and pass the warning on. This RFC sets out the states each router keeps, the messages it sends, and the alarm it raises towards the customer, so that routers from different makers react in the same way.

how do pseudowires signal attachment circuit faults
subtitle: How a provider edge router passes fault warnings between a pseudowire and the customer circuit it emulates.

tldr.problem: A pseudowire carries a native service such as ATM, Frame Relay, TDM or SONET/SDH across a packet network. When the customer circuit or the pseudowire breaks, the routers at both ends have to find out, or they keep sending traffic into a path that no longer works.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives each provider edge four defect states to track, two ways of mapping native service alarms onto pseudowire notifications, and the exact message each state must produce: an LDP status TLV, an L2TP circuit status AVP, or BFD diagnostic codes.
tldr.outcome: Routers from different vendors then raise the same alarms and take the same actions for the same failures, for single-segment pseudowires over MPLS, MPLS/IP and L2TPv3/IP networks.

facts.value: 4: AC receive, AC transmit, PW receive, PW transmit

facts.value: 2: single emulated OAM loop, coupled OAM loops

today: RFC 6310 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2011, and the unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it. Ethernet pseudowires are outside its scope and are covered by a separate document.

sections.title: Why Defects Need a Common Mapping
sections.content:
A pseudowire (PW) carries a native service, such as ATM, Frame Relay, Time Division Multiplexing (TDM) or Synchronous Optical Network / Synchronous Digital Hierarchy (SONET/SDH), across a packet switched network (PSN). At each end a provider edge (PE) connects a customer-facing attachment circuit (AC) to the PW, and the two ACs together form the end-to-end emulated service.

The RFC covers the case where the PW and its ACs are of the same type, so that a homogeneous PW service can be built as described in the PWE3 architecture (RFC 3985). Its objective is to standardize the behaviour of PEs, so that there is no ambiguity about which alarms are raised and which actions are taken in response to a particular failure. It is motivated by the requirements in RFC 4377 and RFC 3916.

The scope is limited in three ways. It covers PWs over MPLS, MPLS/IP and L2TPv3/IP packet networks, and the ATM, Frame Relay, TDM and SONET/SDH services carried over them; the Ethernet PW service is handled in a separate document because of its own characteristics. It gives procedures for PWs set up with the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP, RFC 4447) or L2TPv3 (RFC 3931); fault reporting for PWs established by other means is mentioned but not detailed. And it is scoped to single-segment PWs, although the mechanisms could also be applied to the terminating PEs of multi-segment PWs (RFC 5254).
sections.plainLanguage: A pseudowire carries an older kind of connection, such as ATM or Frame Relay, across a packet network. When something breaks, both ends have to learn about it and warn the customer. This RFC says exactly what each router must record, what message it sends, and what alarm it raises, so that routers from different makers react in the same way.

sections.title: The Reference Model and Where Faults Can Occur
sections.content:
Figure 1 of the RFC shows two customer edges, CE1 and CE2, each attached to a provider edge, PE1 and PE2, by attachment circuits, with one or more pseudowires crossing the packet switched network between the two provider edges. The procedures are written from the point of view of PE1, so the native service network N1 at the near end is local and N2 at the far end is remote.

The RFC then names seven places where a defect can occur. A defect in network N1, including any defect at CE1, that affects all or some of the ACs attached to PE1 is a local AC defect, and it reaches PE1 through the native service's own OAM defect indications. A defect on a PE1 AC interface is another local AC defect, and a defect on a PE1 PSN interface is a third location. A defect inside the PSN itself, affecting all or some of the pseudowires between PE1 and PE2, is conveyed to the PE using a PSN and/or a PW specific OAM defect indication; both data plane and control plane defects have to be taken into account, because a control plane defect can affect the PW status even when the control messages follow a different path from the data. The remaining three locations are the mirror images at the far end: the PE2 PSN interface, the PE2 AC interface, and network N2 including CE2.
sections.plainLanguage: The picture the RFC uses has a customer router at each end, a provider router next to it, and one or more pseudowires between the two provider routers. It names seven places where a fault can start: in either customer network, on either customer-facing circuit, on either provider router's network-facing port, or inside the packet network in between. A fault in the middle can affect every pseudowire at once, so the routers must watch the data path and the control path.

sections.title: The Four Defect States
sections.content:
Each PE tracks four defect states, one for each combination of side and direction: AC receive, AC transmit, PW receive and PW transmit. The arrows in Figure 2 of the RFC show the direction of the user traffic that each state affects.

The states are separated by direction. A transmit defect is any defect that uniquely affects traffic the observing PE sends or relays. A receive defect is any defect that affects information transfer to the observing PE. Because a receive defect also affects traffic that was going to be relayed, it incorporates two defect states, and when a PE is in both a receive and a transmit defect state of the same PW service, the receive defect takes precedence for the consequent actions.

The notifications have a direction as well. A forward defect indication (FDI) is sent in the same direction as the user traffic the defect affects, and a reverse defect indication (RDI) is sent in the direction opposite to that traffic. A PE detects receive defects itself or is told about them: it can be notified of an AC receive defect by an FDI such as an ATM Alarm Indication Signal from CE1, and of a PW receive defect by an FDI from PE2. It cannot detect transmit defects by itself, so it must be notified of those, by an RDI from the far end.
sections.plainLanguage:
Each router remembers four things: a fault on the customer line going in, a fault on the customer line going out, a fault on the tunnel going in, and a fault on the tunnel going out. A fault that affects traffic arriving at the router is more serious than one that affects traffic leaving it, because arriving traffic is also traffic the router was going to pass on. When both apply, the incoming fault wins.

Warnings are directional too. A forward defect indication travels with the affected traffic, so the far end hears about a fault before the traffic reaches it. A reverse defect indication travels against the traffic, so the far end hears that the traffic it sent may not have arrived.

sections.title: Two Ways to Map Native Service Alarms
sections.content:
A homogeneous PW service forwards packets between an AC and a PW of the same type, so it implements both the native service (NS) OAM mechanisms and the PW OAM mechanisms. The RFC defines two modes, which differ only in the method of mapping between the NS and PW OAM defect notification messages.

In the single emulated OAM loop mode, a single end-to-end NS OAM loop is emulated by transparently passing NS OAM messages over the PW. The upstream PE MUST relay those messages unchanged. It MUST signal local defects affecting its AC with an NS defect notification sent over the PW, or with a PW defect notification if the defect stops it generating NS OAM messages. It MUST signal local defects affecting the PW with a PW defect notification. The downstream PE MUST insert NS defect notification messages into its local AC when it detects or is notified of a defect in the PW or in the remote AC, which includes translating a received PW defect notification into an NS defect notification. The PW OAM messages themselves are carried in LDP messages or in the associated channel, not inside the PW.

In the coupled OAM loops mode, three OAM loops are joined at the AC and PW boundaries of the PEs, and NS OAM messages are never carried over the PW. The upstream PE MUST terminate a received NS defect notification and translate it into a PW defect notification, and MUST use PW defect notifications for local AC failures and for local PW failures. The downstream PE behaves as in the first mode.

The default depends on the service. The single emulated loop is the default for all ATM cell mode PW services and the only mode specified for circuit emulation (CEP) and for the SAToP and CESoPSN TDM services, and it is optional for the ATM AAL5 PDU transport and AAL5 SDU transport modes. The coupled loops mode is the default for the Frame Relay, ATM AAL5 PDU transport and AAL5 SDU transport services, optional for ATM VCC cell mode services, and not specified for TDM, CEP or ATM VPC cell mode PW services. A pure coupled mode is not possible for ATM VPC cell mode, because a PE MUST transparently pass VC-level (F5) ATM OAM cells over the PW while terminating and translating VP-level (F4) cells.
sections.plainLanguage:
There are two ways to connect the alarm systems of the customer line and of the tunnel. In the first, one end-to-end alarm loop is emulated: the native alarm messages are carried across the tunnel untouched, and the far router turns tunnel alarms back into native ones. In the second, three separate loops meet at the tunnel ends: the upstream router converts each native alarm into a tunnel alarm, and the downstream router converts tunnel alarms back into native ones.

Which one is used depends on the service. The first is the default for ATM cell mode and the only choice for circuit emulation and the two TDM services. The second is the default for Frame Relay and for the two ATM transport modes.

sections.title: Carrying the Notification
sections.content:
Over MPLS and MPLS/IP, a PE that establishes the PW with LDP and has negotiated use of the LDP status TLV MUST use that TLV for AC and PW status and defect notification. A PE that establishes the PW by static configuration or with BGP MUST support some alternative method of status reporting, and may use BFD for both fault detection and status notification. Over L2TPv3/IP, a PE SHOULD use the Circuit Status Attribute Value Pair (AVP) as the mechanism, and may instead use the Stop-Control-Connection-Notification and Call Disconnect Notify messages to tear down sessions when the extended circuit status is not supported.

The LDP status TLV carries the code points defined in RFC 4446: 0x00000000 for pseudowire forwarding, which clears all failures, and 0x00000001 for pseudowire not forwarding, used when a defect is detected that the other code points do not represent. The four fault codes are 0x00000002 local attachment circuit ingress receive fault, 0x00000004 local attachment circuit egress transmit fault, 0x00000008 local PSN-facing PW ingress receive fault and 0x00000010 local PSN-facing PW egress transmit fault. The RFC maps these onto its two indications: an FDI is the logical OR of the local AC ingress receive fault, the local PSN-facing PW egress transmit fault and pseudowire not forwarding, while an RDI is the logical OR of the local AC egress transmit fault and the local PSN-facing PW ingress receive fault. The same mapping applies to the L2TP Circuit Status AVP, with the addition that a PE MUST set the Active bit to clear all faults and MUST clear it to convey any defect that the specific circuit status flags cannot represent.

Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) can also carry the notification. The connectivity verification (CV) types, negotiated in the OAM capability TLV or the VCCV AVP, decide how it is used. CV types 0x04 and 0x10 mean BFD is used for PW fault detection only, and then only the diagnostic codes 0 (no diagnostic), 1 (control detection time expired), 3 (neighbor signalled session down) and 7 (administratively down) are used. CV types 0x08 and 0x20 mean BFD is used for fault detection and for status notification, adding diagnostic code 6 (concatenated path down) and 8 (reverse concatenated path down). The RFC maps the FDI to diagnostic code 6 together with pseudowire not forwarding, and the RDI to diagnostic code 8. The CV types 0x08 and 0x20 SHOULD NOT be used when the PW is established with the LDP or L2TP control plane.
sections.plainLanguage:
The notification itself travels in one of three mechanisms, chosen by the network underneath. Over MPLS with LDP signalling it is the status field of an LDP message. Over L2TP it is the circuit status field. BFD, the fast liveness check, can also carry it, and the two ends agree beforehand whether BFD is only used to detect failures or also to report them.

The LDP mechanism uses a short list of numeric codes, one for each kind of fault and its direction. The BFD mechanism uses diagnostic codes: 0 for normal, 1 for a timeout, 3 when the far end is going down, and 7 when an operator takes the tunnel down deliberately.

sections.title: Entering and Leaving a Defect State
sections.content:
PE1, as the downstream PE, enters the PW receive defect state when it receives an FDI from PE2 indicating a receive defect on the remote AC or that PE2 detected or was notified of a downstream PW fault, when it detects loss of connectivity on the PSN tunnel upstream of it, or when it detects a loss of PW connectivity through VCCV-BFD or VCCV-Ping. It exits that state when all previously detected defects have disappeared and PE2 has cleared the FDI, if applicable. If the control session between the two PEs fails, the PW is torn down and has to be re-established, but the actions taken towards the ACs are the same as for the receive defect state.

PE1, as the upstream PE, enters the PW transmit defect state when it receives an RDI from PE2 indicating a transmit fault on the remote AC or that PE2 detected or was notified of an upstream PW fault, and it is not already in the PW receive defect state. It exits the transmit defect state when it receives an OAM message from PE2 clearing the RDI, or when it enters the PW receive defect state. For a PW over L2TPv3/IP using the basic Circuit Status AVP, the PW transmit defect state is not valid and a PE can only enter the PW receive defect state.
sections.plainLanguage: The downstream router enters the tunnel receive fault when the far end warns it, when it loses the tunnel, or when the liveness check fails. It leaves that state when the faults are gone and the far end has withdrawn its warning. The upstream router enters the tunnel transmit fault when the far end tells it that traffic it sent will not arrive, but only if it is not already in the receive fault state, because that state matters more.

sections.title: Rules for ATM, Frame Relay, TDM and Circuit Emulation
sections.content:
Each service type has its own entry and exit criteria, because each native service detects faults in its own way. For ATM, the RFC lists the end-to-end and segment F4 and F5 Alarm Indication Signal flows, the reverse defect indication flows, the loss of connectivity found while terminating continuity check cells, and physical layer faults on the ATM interface. On entry to the PW receive defect state the PE MUST commence AIS insertion into the corresponding AC and MUST cease generation of continuity check cells; on entry to the PW transmit defect state it MUST commence RDI insertion into the AC. A PE that detects a PW fault without having received an FDI from PE2 MUST assume PE2 does not know and MUST notify it by sending an RDI, and the mirror case is an FDI.

Frame Relay has no AC transmit defect state, because a Frame Relay data link connection is either up or down with no distinction between directions; to reach the same behaviour as the other technologies, down is represented as a receive defect. A PVC that the Frame Relay network reports as inactive in a full status report, a Link Integrity Verification that shows the link from the PE to the Frame Relay network is down, and a physical layer alarm on the FR interface each put the PE into the AC receive defect state. The A (Active) bit of the full status report carries the result.

Time Division Multiplexing and circuit emulation are real-time services, so the RFC rules out messaging protocols, because they would add delay. Instead it uses the known constant rate of the packets: the PE enters the PW receive defect state when a preconfigured number of TDM PW packets fail to arrive in time, and exits it when the packets once again arrive at their proper rate. The TDM control word carries the flags: the L bit is an AC forward defect indication, the R bit is a PW reverse defect indication, and the M field may modify the meaning of receive defects. On entry to the PW receive defect state the PE MUST commence AIS insertion into the TDM AC and MUST set the R bit in the packets it sends back; on entry to the AC receive defect state it SHOULD overwrite the TDM data with AIS and MUST set the L bit. Circuit emulation works the same way, with the addition that loss of pointer is signalled by the combination of the N and P bits, and that the PE enters the PW receive defect state when it loses packet synchronisation.
sections.plainLanguage:
Each kind of connection detects faults in its own way, so the RFC lists separate rules for each one. ATM has alarm signals, reverse defect signals and continuity check cells, and the router inserts an alarm into the customer line when it enters a fault state. Frame Relay is simpler: its link is either up or down with no direction, so the RFC treats down as an incoming fault and reports it in the Active bit of a status report.

The two real-time services, TDM and circuit emulation, cannot use messages, because a message would arrive too late. They use the timing of the packets instead: if the expected number of packets does not arrive, the link is broken. A flag in the packet header carries the warning in both directions.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The mapping messages described in the RFC do not change the security functions inherent in the messages they carry, so the generic security considerations applicable to PW traffic in Section 10 of RFC 3985 apply to the NS OAM messages transferred inside the PW. The security considerations for VCCV in Section 10 of RFC 5085 apply to the OAM messages transferred that way, and the PWE3 control protocol security considerations in Section 8.2 of RFC 4447 apply to the OAM indications transferred using the LDP status message.

Because the mechanisms enable OAM messages and fault conditions to be propagated between the native service networks and the PSNs, continuity of the end-to-end service depends on a trust relationship between the operators of these networks. The security considerations for that case are discussed in Section 7 of RFC 5254.
sections.plainLanguage: The document adds no new security rules of its own: the rules for the messages it carries still apply. It does point out one dependency. Since faults and alarms now cross between the customer network and the packet network, the end-to-end service only stays up if the two operators trust each other. The security rules for that arrangement are in RFC 5254.

messages.label: FDI
messages.note: Forward defect indication: travels with the affected traffic, warning the far end that the traffic may not arrive.

messages.label: RDI
messages.note: Reverse defect indication: travels against the affected traffic, warning the far end that what it sent may not have arrived.

viz.caption: LDP STATUS TLV CODE POINTS FOR PSEUDOWIRE STATUS

items.label: Pseudowire not forwarding
items.desc: A defect was detected that the other code points do not represent.

items.label: Local AC ingress receive fault
items.desc: The local attachment circuit cannot deliver traffic to the PE.

items.label: Local AC egress transmit fault
items.desc: The local attachment circuit cannot carry traffic away from the PE.

items.label: Local PSN-facing PW ingress receive fault
items.desc: The pseudowire cannot deliver traffic to the PE.

items.label: Local PSN-facing PW egress transmit fault
items.desc: The pseudowire cannot carry traffic away from the PE.

viz.caption: BFD DIAGNOSTIC CODES USED FOR PSEUDOWIRE FAULTS

items.label: No diagnostic
items.desc: The PE is correctly receiving BFD control messages.

items.label: Control detection time expired
items.desc: The PE has stopped receiving BFD control messages and will declare the PW down in the receive direction.

items.label: Neighbor signalled session down
items.desc: The PE confirms to its peer that the BFD session is going down.

items.label: Concatenated path down
items.desc: Used with CV types 0x08 and 0x20 to signal the forward defect indication.

items.label: Administratively down
items.desc: The PW was brought down administratively.

items.label: Reverse concatenated path down
items.desc: Used with CV types 0x08 and 0x20 to signal the reverse defect indication.
